questions.stem: A 57-year-old man was brought into the Emergency Department in a state of collapse. He was known to have end-stage liver disease. He had been bitten on the calf by a neighbor’s dog 5 days beforehand. He had not sought medical care immediately following the injury. On examination, he was profoundly unwell. His temperature was 35.2°C, blood pressure 72/42 mmHg, heart rate 142 beats/min, GCS 14/15. There were multiple purpuric lesions over his torso and limbs. The bite injury was scabbed but clean, with no pus or erythema. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 30 mL/min Lactate 4.6 mmol/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Capnocytophaga canimorsus Capnocytophaga canimorsus, commonly found in canine oral flora, can cause bacteremia and fulminant sepsis in humans, particularly those with asplenia or underlying liver disease. All of the organisms may be involved in bite injury infections, whether human, dog, or cat bite.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q28

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman was bitten by a Rhesus macaque on the forearm. The wound was thoroughly irrigated after the injury, and she was started on amoxicillin/clavulanate.
questions.lead_in: What other prophylactic agent should she be offered?
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Monkey bites involving macaques carry the risk for transmission of B virus, a herpesvirus that can cause fatal encephalomyelitis in humans. Postexposure prophylaxis with either aciclovir or valaciclovir is appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q28

questions.question: You are called about a man attacked by a dog. What interventions would you recommend right now?
questions.question_raw: You are called about a man attacked by a dog.

parts.text: What interventions would you recommend right now?

parts_raw.text: What interventions would you recommend right now?

questions.model_answer: (1) Local wound care: irrigate copiously with water, debride devitalized/necrotic tissue, remove foreign bodies, assess nerve/tendon function and signs of infection; obtain aerobic and anaerobic cultures if infected. (2) Wound closure: avoid primary closure of small/puncture wounds (higher infection risk) — leave to close by secondary intention or delayed primary closure; large/facial wounds may be sutured after irrigation with prophylaxis. (3) Antimicrobial prophylaxis with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for 3-5 days if a selected higher-risk wound (moderate-to-severe injury, preexisting edema/crush, bone/joint or deep hand wound, immunocompromised/asplenic, near a prosthetic joint or genitals). (4) Tetanus immunization if indicated. (5) Rabies risk assessment per rabies guidelines (animal type, provoked vs unprovoked, vaccination/quarantine status, local prevalence) and give rabies immunoglobulin plus vaccine if indicated. (6) Obtain plain radiographs if bony penetration is possible; elevate/immobilize (splint) significant hand injuries; arrange 48-hour follow-up and report to public health if required.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific rabies immunoglobulin dose/vaccine schedule is from CDC/PHAC rabies guidance, not this Mandell text.

cohort_answer.text: Local wound care (cleansing with soap/water and antiseptic, remove foreign bodies, do not suture closed); consider antimicrobial prophylaxis (Clavulin x3-5 days) if high risk area/close to bone-joint/vascular-lymphatic insufficiency/deep puncture or crush injury; surgical consult if evidence of infection; asplenic patients always get prophylaxis; tetanus prophylaxis; risk assessment for rabies (dog's vaccination status, wild/domestic, local prevalence); quarantine dog 10 days and observe; if high risk (rabid dog) consider Rabies Ig 20 IU/kg + rabies vaccine (4 doses 0,3,7,14); report to public health

questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents following a cat bite sustained while playing aggressively with a cat. On examination there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema.
questions.question_raw: You see a 6 year-old child presenting following a cat bite, who he was playing “aggressively” with. On examination, there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema

parts.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for the pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months of age?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive and has received all of his routine immunizations except for the pre-school boosters?

parts_raw.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?

questions.model_answer:
a) Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (first choice for preemptive/prophylactic therapy of terrestrial animal bites); a cat puncture wound is an indication for prophylaxis given the high infection risk and Pasteurella multocida carriage.
b) A puncture bite is a tetanus-prone (not clean-minor) wound. He has had 3 or more prior doses (primary series complete, only the pre-school booster missing), so give a single dose of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (as the due booster); tetanus immune globulin (TIG) is NOT required.
c) Having received vaccines only to 4 months means fewer than 3 doses (2 doses). For a tetanus-prone wound with fewer than 3 (or uncertain) prior doses, give tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine AND TIG, and complete/continue the primary immunization series.
d) HIV positive counts as impaired immunity: an individual with humoral/immune deficiency who has a wound that is not clean and minor should receive BOTH the tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (the due booster) AND TIG, regardless of time since the last dose.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tetanus toxoid/TIG decision rules (dose thresholds, TIG in immunocompromised) are from the Canadian Immunization Guide, not the Mandell text.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents after a cat bite sustained while playing too aggressively with the family cat. The bite is two puncture marks on the arm, clean with no surrounding erythema.

parts.text: If no drug allergies, what is the preferred prophylactic antibiotic?

parts_raw.text: If no drug allergies, what is the preferred prophylactic antibiotic? (0.5)
If the childhood immunizations were up to date except for pre-school boosters. What would you do with regards to tetanus (0.5)
If the child had only received vaccines up to and including 4 months old - what do you do for tetanus in this situation (1)
If the child was HIV+ and immunizations and was UTD except for pre-school boosters, what do you do for tetanus (1)

questions.model_answer:
a) Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (first-choice agent; covers Pasteurella, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and anaerobes).
b) A puncture bite is tetanus-prone. With 3 or more prior doses (primary series done, only pre-school booster missing), give the due tetanus toxoid-containing booster; no TIG.
c) Vaccines only to 4 months = fewer than 3 doses: give tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine AND TIG, and continue/complete the primary series (an accelerated schedule can be used).
d) HIV positive (impaired humoral immunity): for a wound that is not clean and minor, give both the tetanus toxoid-containing booster AND TIG regardless of time since the last dose.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tetanus toxoid/TIG dose thresholds and the TIG rule for humoral immunodeficiency are from the Canadian Immunization Guide, not the Mandell text.

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotic: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (second line TMP/SMX or ceftriaxone + clindamycin, Redbook). Indications for prophylaxis: Immunocompromised; Cat bites; Puncture wounds; Hand, foot or genital involvement; Moderate or severe wounds especially with baseline edema/crush injury; Deep or surgically closed facial wounds. TIG only given if not received 3 dose series previously, or has humoral immune deficiency regardless of immunization status (including heme malignancies and HIV) if wound not minor/clean. Pre-school boosters missing: Give booster as due, no TIG. Only vaccinated to 4 months (2 doses): Need to vaccinate (restart series) and give TIG; can do accelerated course (4 weeks between doses 1,2,3 and 6-12 months between dose 3-4 and 4-5; dose 5 not needed if child over 4 years, so 3 doses 4 weeks apart then 4th booster 6 months later). HIV+ with pre-school boosters missing: Give booster dose and TIG. 'Individuals with humoral immune deficiency who have wounds that are not minor and clean should receive both TIG and tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine, regardless of the time elapsed since the last booster'
